editorialPolicy: Generic public education only; never use personal conversations or private medical history; medical claims require linked primary authoritative evidence and human/clinical review before publication; no affiliate links in medical evidence sections.

health.title: Diabetes: type 1 and type 2
health.summary: Diabetes means blood glucose is too high, but type 1 and type 2 have different causes and treatments.
points: Type 1 is an autoimmune condition. Insulin is essential; dietary changes do not replace it.
Type 2 involves insulin resistance and/or insufficient insulin. Management may include food, activity, medicines and glucose monitoring.
Unexplained thirst, frequent urination, fatigue or weight loss warrant prompt assessment. New symptoms with vomiting, confusion or rapid breathing need emergency assessment.
health.caution: Do not assume a person's diabetes type from age or body weight.

health.title: Type 1 diabetes: an essential guide
health.summary: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition in which the body cannot produce enough insulin; regular insulin treatment is essential.
points: Symptoms can develop quickly: needing to urinate, thirst, tiredness and unexpected weight loss.
Daily insulin, glucose monitoring and education in food/activity effects are core parts of management.
Diabetic ketoacidosis can become life-threatening. Vomiting, abdominal pain, deep breathing or confusion with diabetes symptoms call for emergency help.
health.caution: Fasting or supplements must never replace insulin; discuss major diet changes with the specialist diabetes team.

health.title: Type 2 diabetes: what helps?
health.summary: Type 2 diabetes involves insulin resistance and/or reduced insulin production; management is individual and may include lifestyle change and medicines.
points: The NHS emphasises healthy eating, movement, weight management when appropriate, and prescribed medication.
Complication prevention includes blood pressure, cholesterol, kidney, eye and foot checks.
Remission is possible for some people, but it is not a universal cure and does not justify stopping prescribed medicine independently.
health.caution: Seek prompt advice for new foot pain, swelling, ulcers or rapidly worsening glucose-related symptoms.

health.title: Intermittent fasting: benefits and risks
health.summary: Intermittent fasting changes when people eat; it may help some people control energy intake or weight, but results vary and it is not suitable for everyone.
points: Common approaches include time-restricted eating and alternate-day variations; there is no single best plan for all people.
People taking insulin or medicines that can cause low glucose should seek medication advice before fasting.
A balanced diet, hydration and a sustainable routine matter more than a fashionable fasting label.
health.caution: Pregnancy, eating disorder history, frailty and some medical treatments require individual clinical advice before fasting.

health.title: Supplements: what is worth checking?
health.summary: Supplements can correct specific shortfalls, but many marketed benefits are unproven and excessive doses can cause harm.
points: In the UK, adults are advised to consider 10 micrograms of vitamin D daily in autumn and winter; some groups need it year-round.
Vitamin B12, iron or other nutrients may need assessment where deficiency risk or symptoms exist.
A claimed benefit is not the same as a verified clinical outcome. Check dose, interactions, quality and authorised marketing claims.
health.caution: Do not use supplements instead of prescribed treatment. Ask a pharmacist about possible interactions.

health.title: Gut microbiome: fibre, inulin, GOS and butyrate
health.summary: Dietary fibres feed different gut microbes. Fermentation can produce short-chain fatty acids, including acetate, propionate and butyrate, but effects vary between people.
points: Prebiotic fibres include inulin, fructo-oligosaccharides and galacto-oligosaccharides (GOS). Food sources include leeks, onions, beans and some artichokes.
Increasing fibre too quickly can cause gas and bloating; smaller portions and gradual increases are often better tolerated.
Butyrate is one product of fermentation, not proof that a specific supplement prevents or cures disease. Research outcomes are variable.
health.caution: Vinegar contains acetic acid but is not an established substitute for dietary fibre or a proven way to restore the microbiome after antibiotics.

sources.title: Nature Reviews Microbiology: Fibres and gut microbiome
Review: Prebiotic fibres and individual response (2026)

health.title: Antibiotics, gut bacteria and diabetes claims
health.summary: Antibiotics can disturb gut microbes, but it has not been established that doxycycline itself causes type 2 diabetes.
points: Observational studies have found associations between antibiotic exposure and subsequent diabetes, but these cannot prove the antibiotic caused the condition.
Doxycycline is a tetracycline-class antibiotic, but medicines in the same class may differ in effects and exposure; avoid assuming identical risks.
There is no validated prescription of extra fibre, vinegar, GOS, protein or butyrate that reliably prevents antibiotic-associated metabolic effects.
health.caution: Never stop, avoid or self-start an antibiotic based on a microbiome hypothesis. Antibiotics can be essential for treating serious bacterial infections.

sources.title: Systematic review: Antibiotics and type 2 diabetes association

health.title: Stretching and calisthenics at home
health.summary: Simple, comfortable movements and body-weight exercises can support flexibility, strength and balance, without expensive equipment.
points: Start at a level that matches current mobility and choose a stable support for standing exercises.
Slowly increase repetitions and include movements for strength, balance and flexibility rather than aggressive stretching.
Stop activity that makes pain worse or causes dizziness, numbness or new weakness; seek professional assessment for concerning symptoms.
health.caution: Anyone with recent injury, neurological symptoms or unexplained significant pain should obtain tailored physiotherapy/clinical advice.

health.title: Tai Chi: gentle movement and balance
health.summary: Tai Chi uses slow, controlled movements and attention to posture and balance; it may provide an accessible route into regular physical activity.
points: It can form part of strength, balance and flexibility activity, particularly for older adults.
Choose a suitable beginner class and adapt standing positions to personal ability.
Progress gradually and use nearby stable support if unsteady; activities should not increase pain.
health.caution: Claims that Tai Chi cures medical conditions should be treated cautiously. Evidence and individual results vary.

sources.title: NHS: Physical activity guidelines older adults

health.title: Back and neck pain: where to start
health.summary: Most back and neck pain is non-specific and often improves, but persistent, severe or neurological symptoms need assessment.
points: Gentle activity and adapting daily tasks often help uncomplicated back pain.
Possible causes include muscular strain, joint or disc problems and sometimes nerve irritation; symptoms alone rarely pinpoint one tissue.
New bladder or bowel dysfunction, numbness around the genitals or bottom, or severe progressive leg weakness are emergency warning signs.
health.caution: High fever, rapidly worsening pain or feeling seriously unwell with back pain can signal infection: seek urgent assessment.

health.title: Lumbar back pain and sciatica
health.summary: Lower-back pain can arise from several structures, and sciatica describes pain or neurological symptoms related to nerve irritation.
points: Stay as active as reasonably possible; avoid prolonged bed rest for uncomplicated episodes.
A clinician can assess whether self-management, physiotherapy or specialist review is appropriate.
Imaging is not routinely needed for every episode; severe or progressive neurological signs change the urgency.
health.caution: Seek emergency help for new bladder/bowel difficulties, saddle numbness or severe/progressive weakness, especially with bilateral symptoms.

sources.title: NICE NG59: Low back pain and sciatica

health.title: Modic changes: inflammation, bacteria and antibiotics
health.summary: Modic changes are MRI findings at vertebral endplates. A low-grade bacterial explanation has been proposed for some cases but remains contested.
points: Type 1 changes generally reflect bone-marrow oedema/inflammatory signal; type 2 changes predominantly fatty marrow signal.
Cutibacterium acnes, a common skin bacterium, has been studied as one possible contributor, but biopsy results and causation are disputed.
The larger double-blind AIM trial did not find a clinically important benefit from three months of antibiotics for chronic low-back pain with Modic changes.
health.caution: Having acne or groin boils does not establish a spinal infection. Groin lesions can instead be hidradenitis suppurativa, which requires its own assessment. Do not self-treat Modic changes with doxycycline.

sources.title: NICE: Low back pain and sciatica

health.title: Neck pain and stiffness
health.summary: Neck stiffness is often temporary, although persistent or worsening pain and neurological symptoms should be examined.
points: Gentle movement and simple comfort measures can help uncomplicated neck pain.
Avoid unsafe driving or cycling if you cannot rotate your head properly.
New arm weakness, spreading numbness, gait changes or serious injury warrant medical assessment.
health.caution: Avoid forcing the neck through painful ranges. Seek urgent care when neck pain follows major trauma or accompanies serious neurological symptoms.

sources.title: NHS: Neck pain and stiff neck

health.title: Hip and leg pain: common causes and warning signs
health.summary: Hip and leg pain can involve joints, tendons, muscles, circulation or nerves; an individual examination matters more than guessing from location.
points: Hip stiffness and pain with walking can have several causes, including osteoarthritis or tendon problems.
Pain radiating from the back may be nerve-related; swollen or hot joints raise different concerns.
Balance and strengthening can help some mechanical problems, but should match the diagnosis and symptoms.
health.caution: A hot swollen hip with fever needs urgent assessment; a severe injury with inability to bear weight needs emergency assessment.

health.title: Foot and ankle pain: swelling, balance and diabetes
health.summary: Foot or ankle pain often has a mechanical cause, but new warmth, redness, swelling or loss of sensation can need prompt assessment.
points: Insoles, suitable shoes, gentle mobility and pacing may help some mechanical problems after assessment.
Changes in arch shape, weakness or numbness need assessment rather than a generic exercise plan.
People with diabetes and foot pain or swelling should seek timely professional help.
health.caution: A hot swollen foot, rapidly worsening pain, fever, inability to walk or new colour change requires urgent assessment. Do not assume infection or Charcot without proper evaluation.

health.title: Healthy ageing: strength, balance and function
health.summary: Healthy ageing is less about a miracle compound and more about maintaining strength, mobility, social connection and management of preventable risks.
points: Regular activity supports cardiovascular health, balance and muscle function.
For many older adults, weekly strength, flexibility and balance practice matters alongside aerobic activity.
Claims about biological-age reversal, longevity supplements or anti-ageing treatments require higher-quality human outcome evidence.
health.caution: Match activity to ability, and discuss significant new symptoms or major programme changes with a clinician.

sources.title: NHS: Activity guidelines for older adults

health.title: How to check a health claim
health.summary: A convincing mechanism, attractive graph or testimonial does not prove a product meaningfully improves health.
points: Find the exact claim, relevant population, measured outcome and quality of supporting human evidence.
Check whether the claim is about symptoms, a laboratory marker, risk reduction or an actual clinical outcome.
Look for independent replication, conflicts of interest, adverse effects and whether marketing wording is legally authorised.
health.caution: Articles can discuss developing research without converting it into a product advertisement or implying supplements treat disease.

sources.title: ASA/CAP: Food and supplement claim rules

jobs.title: Interview questions: prepare evidence, not scripts
jobs.summary: Prepare examples of decisions, challenges and results using a concise situation-action-result structure; tailor evidence to the job.
points: Read the job description and identify essential skills.
Prepare credible, measurable examples and questions about the role.
Practise answers aloud without memorising a rigid script.
jobs.caution: Check each employer's current process and use original evidence, not invented credentials or roles.

jobs.title: How to research a prospective employer
jobs.summary: Use official company information, current news and job descriptions to test whether the role, team and company are a fit.
points: Start with the company's own site, careers page and filings where relevant.
Cross-check independent news, public product documentation and project history.
Prepare one or two specific questions informed by research; don't present rumours as fact.
jobs.caution: Check each employer's current process and use original evidence, not invented credentials or roles.

sources.title: Companies House: Find and update company information

jobs.title: LinkedIn profile: position yourself for senior roles
jobs.summary: A senior-level LinkedIn profile should communicate the problems you solve, the scale of your work and accountable outcomes.
points: Use a headline that reflects the next role and your strongest specialist value.
Write an About section with responsibilities, business outcomes and relevant technical/leadership experience.
Verify every claim, keyword and achievement; tailor without overstating your experience.
jobs.caution: Check each employer's current process and use original evidence, not invented credentials or roles.
